question: In which fiscal year's 10-K did NVIDIA first mention the EU AI Act in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer:
**FY2024** (NVIDIA's 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 28, 2024).

The first appearance was in Item 1A (Risk Factors), in a sentence added that year: *"Furthermore, the EU AI Act could impose onerous obligations that may disproportionately impact and disadvantage us and require us to change our business practices."* [1]

It then evolved:
- **FY2025:** the EU AI Act language was expanded and moved into a discussion of AI regulation, noting it "became effective on August 1, 2024 and will be fully applicable after a two-year transitional period" [2], while the FY2024 sentence was revised to read "the EU AI Act and similar legislation" [3].
- **FY2026:** both passages carried forward essentially unchanged [4][5].

Note: the claim data covers NVDA's FY2022–FY2026 filings, so FY2024 is the first appearance within that window (and no earlier year in the dataset mentions it).

question: In which fiscal year's 10-K did AMD first mention ZT Systems in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer:
**AMD first mentioned ZT Systems in its FY2024 10-K** (fiscal year ended December 28, 2024) — in both Item 1A (Risk Factors) and Item 7 (MD&A).

- In MD&A, AMD described entering an August 2024 agreement to acquire ZT Group Int'l, Inc. (ZT Systems), a provider of AI and general-purpose compute infrastructure for hyperscale computing companies [12], and framed it as extending its data center infrastructure capabilities [4].
- In Risk Factors, AMD warned that it intended to seek a strategic partner to acquire ZT Systems' manufacturing business and might not realize the anticipated benefits of the transaction [3][14]; it also disclosed a $300 million termination fee in certain circumstances [2].

The claim data covers AMD's FY2021–FY2025 filings and shows **no ZT Systems mentions in FY2021, FY2022, or FY2023** [1].

By FY2025, the language changed to completed acquisition: AMD closed the deal in March 2025 and sold the ZT manufacturing business to Sanmina in October 2025 [7][9][13].

question: NVIDIA used to discuss the terminated Arm acquisition in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7). Which fiscal year's filing was the last to mention it?
answer:
The last filing to mention it in **Item 1A or Item 7** was the **FY2024 10-K** (fiscal year ended January 28, 2024).

Its MD&A discussed the “$1.4 billion acquisition termination charge related to the proposed Arm transaction” recorded in fiscal 2023 [15], including a dedicated “Acquisition Termination Cost” section [16]. The Arm-related claims in that FY2024 MD&A were dropped in the FY2025 filing [8][9].

NVIDIA’s FY2025 10-K still mentioned the termination in **Note 2 to the financial statements**, but not in Item 1A or Item 7 [11].

question: Is COVID-19 still mentioned in the risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7) in Qualcomm's latest 10-K? If not, when did it last appear?
answer:
**No — COVID-19 is no longer mentioned by name in Qualcomm's latest 10-K (FY2025, ended September 28, 2025), in either Item 1A or Item 7.**

**Latest 10-K (FY2025):**
- Item 1A still carries generic pandemic language, but no COVID-19 reference: "health crises, including epidemics or pandemics, and government and business responses thereto, could affect our manufacturing facilities, including by resulting in quarantines and/or closures" [6]; likewise "pandemics or other health crises affecting any of the regions in which we operate" [8] and the risk factor "Geopolitical conflicts, natural disasters, pandemics and other health crises, and other factors outside of our control, could significantly disrupt our business" [10].
- Item 7's forward-looking discussion now focuses on tariffs/trade policy rather than COVID: "We continue to monitor the recent changes in global trade policy, including tariffs and related trade actions announced by the U.S., China and other countries" [21][22].

**When it last appeared:**
- **Item 1A (Risk Factors): FY2023 10-K (ended September 24, 2023)** is the last year with explicit COVID-19 language — e.g., the supply-chain risk factor said "health crises, including epidemics or pandemics, such as the COVID-19 pandemic" [17], the manufacturing-disruption factor used the same phrasing [19], 5G deployment delays were attributed to "the COVID-19 pandemic" [18], and the workplace-practices discussion opened "The COVID-19 pandemic caused us to modify our workforce practices" [16]. In the FY2024 10-K the same passages appear with the COVID-19 references removed ("health crises, including epidemics or pandemics, and government and business responses thereto…") [11][14].
- **Item 7 (MD&A): FY2022 10-K (ended September 25, 2022)** is the last year with explicit COVID-19 discussion — e.g., impairment judgments "due to the continuing effects of the COVID-19 pandemic" [36] and "The degree to which the COVID-19 pandemic impacts our business, financial condition and results of operations will depend on future developments, which are highly uncertain" [37]. By FY2023, MD&A had replaced it with the Israel-Hamas war and macroeconomic weakness discussion [32][34].

So the term dropped out of MD&A after FY2022 and out of Risk Factors after FY2023; the FY2024 and FY2025 filings refer only to "pandemics or other health crises" generically.

question: Which of these companies name TSMC in the risk factors (Item 1A) of their most recent 10-K: AMD, Broadcom, Intel, Microchip, NVIDIA?
answer:
**Yes:** AMD, Broadcom, and Intel. **No:** Microchip and NVIDIA.

| Company | Latest 10-K | Names TSMC in Item 1A? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AMD** | FY2025 | **Yes** | Relies on TSMC for “all wafers for microprocessor and GPU products at 7 nanometer (nm) or smaller nodes” [52]. |
| **Broadcom** | FY2025 | **Yes** | “Approximately 95% of the wafers manufactured by our CMs were produced by TSMC” in fiscal 2025 [55]. |
| **Intel** | FY2025 | **Yes** | Says products may become dependent on third-party foundries, “particularly TSMC,” and that it has no long-term contract with TSMC [58]. |
| **Microchip** | FY2026 | **No** | Its risk factors refer generically to “Taiwan-based third-party wafer foundries” without naming TSMC [16]. |
| **NVIDIA** | FY2026 | **No** | Its Item 1A discusses foundry dependence generically [27]; TSMC is named in Item 1 (Business), not the risk factors [39]. |

So, in their most recent 10-K **Item 1A**, the TSMC-naming companies are **AMD, Broadcom, and Intel**.

question: How did Microsoft's effective tax rate change from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2026? Give each year's figure.
answer:
**Microsoft effective tax rate (fiscal years ended June 30):**

| Fiscal year | Effective tax rate |
|---|---|
| 2022 | 13.1% [1] |
| 2023 | 19.0% [8] |
| 2024 | 18.2% [2]/[22] |
| 2025 | 17.6% [17] |
| 2026 | 19.4% [21] |

**Change 2022 → 2026:** up 6.3 percentage points (from 13.1% to 19.4%), a ~48.1% relative increase [1][21].

- The jump in FY2023 was mainly because FY2022 included a $3.3 billion net tax benefit from transferring intangible properties out of Puerto Rico in Q1 FY2022, plus a decrease in stock-based compensation tax benefits in FY2023 [8].
- FY2024's dip reflected tax benefits from tax law changes, including the delay of the final foreign tax credit regulations [13].
- FY2025's decline and the FY2026 increase were both attributed primarily to changes in the mix of earnings and tax expenses between the U.S. and foreign countries [23].
- Note: FY2026's rate reconciliation was presented under the new ASU 2023-09 format (gross GILTI with foreign tax credits), so the components aren't directly comparable to earlier years, though the effective rate is [21][22].

question: How did Broadcom's risk-factor statement about its largest end customers change between its fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2024 10-Ks?
answer:
**Broadcom's largest-end-customer risk disclosure, FY2023 → FY2024 10-K**

**What it said in FY2023:** The risk factor named Apple explicitly and tied it to the top-five group: "We believe aggregate sales, through all channels, to Apple and our top five end customers, accounted for approximately 20% and 35% of our net revenue for fiscal year 2023, respectively," with a companion sentence stating that sales to Apple Inc. were ~20% of net revenue in each of fiscal 2023 and 2022 [15][18].

**What changed in FY2024:**
- **Apple was dropped as a named customer.** The FY2023 sentence quantifying Apple at ~20% of net revenue is explicitly flagged as not present in the FY2024 filing, and no Apple customer-concentration claim appears in FY2024 (or FY2025) [18].
- **The top-five figure was raised to 40% and framed as a two-year trend:** "We believe aggregate sales to our top five end customers, through all channels, accounted for approximately 40% and 35% of our net revenue for fiscal years 2024 and 2023, respectively" [24] — versus the flat "~35% in each of fiscal 2023 and 2022" language a year earlier [19].
- **The single-customer sentence was rewritten anonymously and scaled up:** FY2023 said "Direct sales to WT Microelectronics Co., Ltd., a distributor, accounted for 21% and 20% of our net revenue for fiscal years 2023 and 2022" [17]; FY2024 replaced the named distributor with "Direct sales to one customer, which is a distributor, accounted for 28% and 21% of our net revenue for fiscal years 2024 and 2023, respectively" [23]. (That disclosure trended further in FY2025 to "one semiconductor solutions customer, which is a distributor," at 32% and 28% [28].)

**Net effect:** between the FY2023 and FY2024 10-Ks, the statement shifted from naming Apple as a ~20% end customer alongside a ~35% top-five aggregate, to an unnamed-customer formulation in which the top five end customers account for ~40% of net revenue and the largest single (distributor) customer rose from 21% to 28% [18][23][24]. Distributor share of net revenue, for context, fell from 57% in FY2023 to 48% in FY2024 [16][22].

question: What were Qualcomm's fiscal 2025 revenues and net income, and what does the filing say about future product revenue from Huawei?
answer:
**Qualcomm fiscal 2025 (year ended September 28, 2025)**

- **Revenues:** $44.28 billion, up 14% from $39.0 billion in fiscal 2024 [1][5]
- **Net income:** $5.54 billion, down 45% from $10.1 billion in fiscal 2024 [2][5]

**Huawei — future product revenue**

The 10-K states that the company expects **no further product revenues from Huawei**: in May 2024 the U.S. Department of Commerce revoked the export license under which Qualcomm had been selling 4G and certain other integrated circuit products to Huawei, and "accordingly, we do not expect to receive any further product revenues from Huawei." It adds that to the extent Huawei's devices take share from OEMs that use Qualcomm's products (in China or elsewhere), results of operations and cash flows could be further impacted [3].

Separately, on the licensing side, QTL revenues **stopped including royalties from Huawei beginning in the second quarter of fiscal 2025**, because Huawei's license agreement has expired [4]. QTL licensing revenues were roughly flat at $5.58 billion in fiscal 2025 versus $5.57 billion in fiscal 2024 [4].

question: What share of Broadcom's contract-manufactured wafers did TSMC make in fiscal 2020?
answer:
**Fiscal 2020 isn't in the available data.** The filing index for Broadcom (AVGO) covers only FY2021–FY2025, and a search restricted to a FY2020 10-K returned no passages. So I can't give you the FY2020 share.

The earliest year disclosed in the available filings is fiscal 2021:

| Broadcom fiscal year | Share of CM-manufactured wafers made by TSMC |
|---|---|
| 2021 | ~89% [1][6] |
| 2022 | ~90% [4][7] |
| 2023 | ~90% [3][8] |
| 2024 | ~95% [5][9] |
| 2025 | ~95% [2][10] |

In each year's risk factors, Broadcom describes TSMC as "one of our CMs" and warns that TSMC also fabricates wafers for competitors and "could choose or be required to prioritize capacity for other customers or reduce or eliminate deliveries to us on short notice" [1][2].
